Tech Report: How to Find Stability and Freedom in Supported Headstand

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 13 min read (2566 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Yogajournal

⏱️ ~13 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that in Yoga Journal’s Archives series, we share a curated collection of articles originally published in past issues beginning in 1975.
  • According to recent reports, “Sthera sukham asanam,” “Posture is steady and comfortable,” says Patanjali in the first of his three sutras on asana.
  • It has been revealed that because balancing in Headstand (Sirsasana) is such a challenge, it forces us to look deeply into our posture and our nervous system to discover an inner sense of balance.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that in Yoga Journal’s Archives series, we share a curated collection of articles originally published in past issues beginning in 1975. This article about Headstand first appeared in the July-August 1990 issue of Yoga Journal. Find more of our Archives here.

According to recent reports, “Sthera sukham asanam,” “Posture is steady and comfortable,” says Patanjali in the first of his three sutras on asana. But as even experienced yoga students know, “steady and comfortable” are not the first words that come to mind to describe the sensation of standing on one’s head. And many couch potatoes would probably insist that they feel quite steady and comfortable as they sprawl out in front of the tube. So what exactly does Patanjali mean by the words sthira and sukham?

It has been revealed that because balancing in Headstand (Sirsasana) is such a challenge, it forces us to look deeply into our posture and our nervous system to discover an inner sense of balance. This interiorization of awareness can reveal some of the subtleties behind Patanjali’s words.

It has been revealed that the word thira comes from the Sanskrit root tha, meaning “to stand,” which is also the root of the English words “stay,” “stable,” and “steady.” This root verb is of great importance in the Yoga Sutras. Patanjali first uses it in defining the term abhyasa, or practice, in Sutra I-13: “Practice is the endeavor toward stillness and stability of the mindfield.” According to Pandit Usharbhud Arya’s commentary, “Meditation means bringing the mind to stillness or stability, which means freedom from the rajasic and tamasic turbulences, the mind’s one-pointed concentration on a single sattic vrtti harmonious vibration remaining uninterrupted so that the mind flows in a calm, pacific, smooth stream.”.

For a hatha yoga practitioner, the following question arises: How can I bring this level of mental stillness into an asana such as Headstand, and, conversely, how can I adjust in the asana to stabilize and deepen the mental stillness? In other words, how can I explore the states of thira and sukham in the pose?

Industry observers note that in previous asana columns, we have looked at the relationship of the bones, the flesh, and the skin to posture, circulation, and breathing. We have seen that the muscle fibers assist in circulation through their pumping action and that when they are open to the free flow of the breath, they can subtly communicate with the inner lining of the skin. Stability and comfort are accompanied by stable, grounded bones, effortless breathing, a fluid feeling of the flesh, and a sensitive inner skin. Fear, insecurity, and instability, on the other hand, are accompanied by hardened muscles, disturbed breathing, restricted blood flow, collapsed joints, and insensitive skin. The question now becomes: How can I organize the bones, muscle fibers, and skin to create a stable posture that allows the breath and bodily fluids to flow freely?

Freedom or restriction of the breath and bodily fluids can be experienced in the expansion, contraction, and inner pressure of the body’s three main cavities: the pelvic-abdominal cavity (from the diaphragm to the pelvic floor), the thoracic cavity, and the skull. In any posture, the respiratory rhythm begins with an expansion of the thoracic cavity, accomplished by the contraction and descent of the diaphragm and the lifting and widening of the rib cage by the intercostal and other respiratory muscles. This expansion creates a negative pressure (lower than normal atmospheric pres sure) in the chest, drawing air from outside the body into the lungs. With the exhalation, a positive pressure (higher than normal atmospheric pressure) is created as the expansion ceases and the elastic recoil of the lung tissue presses the air out of the lungs.

In soft, quiet breathing, there is no resistance to this cycle. The pelvic-abdominal cavity expands and releases in harmony with the thoracic cavity, and air flows in and out of the body without impedence. The expansion and contraction of the body is perfectly matched by the movement of air in and out of the lungs. Because of this balance, the sensation of interior pressure remains constant throughout the body.

However, any unnecessary tension in the body will create resistance to the breath and a corresponding increase in resistance to the circulatory fluids. This resistance creates the sensation of increased internal pressure, a sensation to which the brain and skull are especially sensitive. To experience this sensation in an exaggerated way, inhale, close your mouth, close your nostrils with your fingers, and try to exhale.

Notice the immediate increase in pressure in the brain. Close your mouth and nostrils after exhaling and you will experience a slightly different pressure increase.

According to recent reports, tension anywhere in the body will have a similar pressurizing effect. For example, neck and shoulder tension restricts the expansion of the rib cage, disrupting the respiratory rhythm and increasing the pressure in the skull. Psychological stresses tend to be reflected in a tense diaphragm, and the diaphragm also reacts to tension in the groins and pelvic region. When the groins are open, the bones of the legs, pelvis, and lower spine support the weight of the body, and the muscles of that region are free to expand and contract with the breathing cycle. However, when the groins are restricted, the pelvic floor cannot.

Recent findings suggest that “breathe,” and this resistance in the pelvic-abdominal region impedes the movement of the diaphragm. This constriction of the breath creates pressure in the skull, just as you experienced when you held your mouth and nostrils shut.

In a recent development, standing on one’s head exacerbates all of these restrictions to the breath. The shoulders and neck are often tensed to hold on to the body. Fears of falling tighten the diaphragm. The legs and pelvis are often collapsed and unconscious. Thus the breath will be constricted and the brain will feel pressurized. The most obvious aspect of this syndrome is that blood cannot move out of the skull, leading to a sense of congestion. (Some degree of pressure is usual when first starting to practice Headstand; a beginner should not expect to feel perfectly quiet and comfortable right away. But if the eyes become bloodshot or if extreme pressure is felt in the eyes or ears, the pose is being done incorrectly and should not be held. Seek guidance from a qualified teacher.).

Industry observers note that the increased pressure in the skull results from a breakdown in the pumping system of the body. The diaphragm is a large pump for moving air, and the skeletal muscles must pump fluids back to the heart to maintain circulation. To facilitate these processes of circulation and respiration, the body is organized into six regions, each with its own “relay station” to oversee the movement of fluids and breath in and out of that region. Although most of these relay stations do not have a single specialized physical component like the diaphragmatic muscle, I will refer to them as diaphragms for lack of a better term, because, like the diaphragm, they function as pumps. (The term “diaphragm” is a convenient metaphor for the complex set of physiological and psychological mechanisms that control the movement of fluids, air, and energy in and out of a particular area of the body.

These diaphragms and their powerful effects can be experienced subjectively by turning the attention inward, although most of them cannot be objectively revealed through dissection.) These diaphragmatic regions, as introduced to me by my teacher, Ramanand Patel, are the brain, the throat, the heart, the respiratory diaphragm, the navel, and the pelvic floor.

Industry observers note that in order to attain thira and sukham in Headstand, all six diaphragms must be functioning properly. However, this article will focus on the first and sixth diaphragm, as these are particularly important.

It has been revealed that the sixth diaphragm has a tangible physical component, the muscles of the pelvic floor. Open groins, strong legs, and stable hip joints are necessary for the healthy functioning of this diaphragm, which should move synchronously with the physical diaphragm, creating the sense that the pelvis and abdomen breathe freely:.

In a recent development, correct action of the pelvic diaphragm stabilizes the coccyx bone and helps circulate fluids in and out of the legs. Its location is the first chakra, the chakra of grounding and stability, and thus it plays an important role in developing the quality of shira.

In a recent development, the first diaphragm is the brain or skull diaphragm, responsible for moving energy in the form of blood and cerebrospinal fluid) in and out of the brain. This diaphragm has no muscular components; rather, it is composed of a complex combination of neural pathways and blood vessels. My experience has been that it moves in opposition to the other five diaphragms: When the other five diaphragms are “inhaling,” or drawing energy in, the brain diaphragm is “exhaling,” or releasing. Conversely, when the lower five are exhaling, the brain “inhales.” This is the rhythm that accompanies a healthy nervous and circulatory system, leading to shira and sukham.

However, if the pelvic diaphragm is locked or inhibited, the brain diaphragm will “inhale” along with the torso, leading to an increase in tension in the muscles and pressure in the skull. This tension can also be felt as disturbances in the skin, eyes, ears, and tongue.

Before attempting Headstand, you should have a strong, stable Downward-Facing Dog Pose and a regular standing pose practice to ensure the strength, flexibility, and intelligence of your arms and legs necessary to protect the neck and skull. Use a firm blanket or mat for the head. If possible, learn to balance in a corner of the room, resting one foot on each wall to prevent tilting to one side or another. If a corner is not available, use any wall, placing your hands close to the wall to keep from arching your back into a banana shape.

According to recent reports, place your forearms on the floor, interlocking your fingers evenly and completely and keeping your wrists perpendicular to the floor. Your elbows should be exactly shoulder width apart. This foundation must be stabilized by constant practice.

According to recent reports, in building this foundation, several difficulties may be encountered. One arm may overpower the other, distorting the shoulders, forearms, and wrists and torquing the foundation. Learn to press evenly into both arms. Your wrists may collapse outward, losing their grounding and strength. Consciously hold the thumb side of your wrists toward each other. Your elbows may splay apart. Maintain a constant pressure from your outer elbows toward each other, as if your elbows were pressing into a block held between them. However, do not draw them closer than shoulder width.

Having established this stable foundation, place your head up against your wrists and palms, cupping your skull without losing the strength of the wrists. Taking the weight onto the arms and not the neck, use the strength of the groins and pelvis to lift both legs up from the floor. (Beginners will probably have to throw one leg up at a time, but as soon as possible should begin lifting both at once.) Resting your feet against the wall, lift the weight of the body out of the shoulders, away from the neck.

In a recent development, learning this lifting action is more crucial than learning to balance. Only when the lift is strong and the balance stable should you move to the center of the room.

Students who can balance steadily in the center of the room can begin to explore the effect on the pose of the pelvic and brain diaphragms. Most beginning students look something like the “inverted banana” in Figure 1. Your shoulders sink, the floating ribs and upper lumbar hang forward, your back body collapses, and your legs fall behind the midline. With no vertical extension, the weight of the torso collapses onto your neck and skull, compressing the brain diaphragm. The legs are not lifting, and their weight hardens the posterior pelvic floor and the inner front groins. The anterior coccyx bone hangs unsupported.

It has been revealed that instead, your arms and shoulders must lift actively away from the neck and skull. Figure 2 shows a close-up of the correct lifting action. Note the widening of the upper inner shoulder blades and the lifting of the inner and outer deltoid muscles, which lifts the weight of the torso away from the neck and skull. This action can be learned in Downward-Facing Dog (Adho Mukha Svanasana).

Sources indicate that your legs also must be brought forward, lifting the lumbar, pelvis, and legs to eliminate the banana-like collapse. Intermediate students often learn this action, only to close the anterior pelvis and inner groins and lose the support of the posterior coccyx (see Figure 3). The front and inner groins must be dynamically extended, without collapsing onto the lumbar. Your legs must work tremendously in Headstand to open the pelvic diaphragm. In working the legs, be sure to extend the bones from the pelvis without hardening and tensing the muscles—rather, keep the muscles vibrant. If the leg muscles harden, the pelvic diaphragm will tighten and the brain will become pressurized and confused.

It has been revealed that in the completed position (Figure 5), your front body and back body extend evenly, aligning the bones with gravity. When the bones are aligned, they can support the weight of the body without muscular strain. Figure 4 has been inverted to show the alignment of the arches, knees, hips, shoulders, and ears. By lifting evenly out of the pelvis, the bones of the legs free the pelvic diaphragm to breathe and pump blood to the legs. The dynamic action of the legs lifts the weight of the torso from the skull, allowing the brain diaphragm to breathe.

The anterior and posterior sides of the coccyx bone are supported, freeing the pelvic diaphragm. This freedom allows the respiratory diaphragm to breathe easily, which in turn allows the brain to feel relaxed and spacious. Thus the whole pose feels spacious, stable, and comfortable.

Stability and comfort are prerequisites for deeper work in the poses. As Vyassa indicates in his commentary to the first of the Yoga Sutras, yoga is samadhi. Sthira and sukham are the beginning of the samadhi state and thus are the point at which true yoga commences. All previous action is preparatory in nature. To achieve thira and sukham, it is not sufficient just to sit in any comfortable pose. Rather, you must perfect the pose to such an extent that samadhi can spontaneously awaken.

The universe is alive, awakening and creating itself anew with each moment. If we create the proper foundations of shira and sukham, so that our mind and body are clear and calm, we can directly experience this awakening and creativity. With 10 years until the turn of the millenium, human consciousness is awakening to its own inner potentials as it is simultaneously awakening to the potentials of the natural world. All serious practitioners of yoga should work to be stabilized at least in the beginning level of thira and sukham by then, so we can usher in a upcoming age of planetary awakening, with wisdom, compassion, and ecological communion with the natural world as our goals.

On Cloudsurfer 3 Review: A Firm-Soft Daily Trainer for Long, Easy Miles

📅 13 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (893 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Runnersworld

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that we earn a commission for products purchased through some links in this article.
  • The Cloudsurfer 3 is a real step forward for On, even though it’s most definitely a daily trainer built with max cushioning for easy miles.
  • Right now, it’s only available in-store and at selected retailers, but it releases nationwide February 2027.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that we earn a commission for products purchased through some links in this article. Why Trust Us?

The Cloudsurfer 3 is a real step forward for On, even though it’s most definitely a daily trainer built with max cushioning for easy miles. It doesn’t have the pop of the brand’s bouncier shoes, and I don’t think it’s trying to. What it has in abundance is a steady, firm-soft (not a contradiction) cushion that holds up over long, easy miles, plus a fit that works beautifully for my feet.

Right now, it’s only available in-store and at selected retailers, but it releases nationwide February 2027.

According to recent reports, the headline is Surreal, On’s first supercritical midsole foam, which is EVA-based and sits inside a redesigned CloudTec Phase structure. Supercritical processing infuses the foam with gas under high pressure and temperature, then lets it expand in an autoclave—a machine that uses steam to superheat the environment. That’s the same basic-ish idea behind the “super foams” that have taken over daily trainers, but On had never made it work with its hollow Clouds.

According to recent reports, scott Maguire, president and COO of On, explained why in an interview with Runner-in-Chief Jeff Dengate. “We’ve only ever been able to do CloudTec in EVA in the past,” he remarked. “We’ve never been able to do it in a supercritical processing.”.

In a recent development, the trouble was scale. “Putting Clouds in that, it becomes super small and it has to become very major,” Maguire said. Predicting where each Cloud will form, how far apart they sit, and how they interact “has been impossible for us to do for years.”.

It has been revealed that on’s own numbers put Surreal at roughly 15 percent softer, 15 percent lighter, and 23.3 percent more responsive than Helion, the foam that came before Surreal. The redesigned CloudTec Phase geometry is credited with 15.5 percent deeper compression and a 9.9 percent cut in peak braking force. Those figures come from finite element analysis simulations at On Labs Zurich, so they are modeled results, not data from everyday runners; a grain of salt should be well-applied. What I felt in the ride was a foam that’s soft but has a firm backbone, kind of like a good honeycomb-cushion feeling.

Here’s where my opinion comes in. The newly introduced foam is an improvement, but the return doesn’t have quite the oomph of other shoes in On’s lineup. If you’re hoping for a springy kickoff, look elsewhere.

In a recent development, what I love is the character of the cushion. It’s firm-softness—if that’s a thing—which I declare it is. Over long miles, it never felt like it compacted, and it never gave so much that it slowed me down. Since I run more miles than speed, that’s my best case.

It has been revealed that dengate, who has been tough on On’s hole-based tech in the past because slabs of modern foam were beating it, came around: The Cloudsurfer 3 “really does feel like a big improvement in comfort and ride for a daily training shoe.” Gear Editor Amanda Furrer, who admits she found past On trainers kind of blah, rated this one near-perfect. As a cushioned trainer, she noted she’d have to quote me, saying: “it’s aces.”.

Sources indicate that on gets fit so right. From its super shoes to its ultra trail runners like the Cloudultra Pro, they’re somehow both forgiving and secure, with a heel-lock eyelet placement that’s my personal favorite bit of the brand. (That, and the Zendaya commercials. I love her.).

Recent findings suggest that I have high arches and a correspondingly high instep, and this shoe suits both. There was no rubbing and no hot spots, and I never felt the need to loosen my laces at the midfoot. The warp-knit upper is plush through the collar and tongue and secure without clamping or getting that weird bunching pleat thing that I loathe.

Recent findings suggest that furrer saw the same thing from the wide-foot side. For runners with wide feet and high insteps, she says, the “Cloudsurfer is fitted and not tight, but also secure.”.

According to recent reports, this is not a speedwork shoe. If you want a rocket for tempo days, keep looking. It’s also on the heavier side, which is the trade-off for all that stack.

It has been revealed that but as an everyday trainer for long, easy miles, it’s excellent. The foam is better, the fit is better, and the ride stays consistent from the first mile to the last. For high-arched runners especially, I’d put it near the top of the try-on list.

Shop Men’s at marathonsports.com | Shop Women’s at marathonsports.com.

For over a decade, she has tested parenting, fitness, home, and running gear and written in-depth guides to help readers with their next purchase. Holding multiple advanced degrees and currently studying kinesiology, Cat Bowen brings research-backed insight to all of her guides. Passionate about women’s health and neurodivergent inclusion, she advocates for closing research gaps and helping others—especially AudHD people—find joy in running and fitness.

#68489. Triathlon as the New Run Club: Community Without “Bro Culture”

📅 18 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 15m • 📚 Deep Dive (2956 w)

Triathlon as the New Run Club: Community Without “Bro Culture”

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 15 min read (2956 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Triathlete

⏱️ ~15 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Triathlon club founders and disruptors share how they are building inclusive communities.
  • What do you do when you’re fed up with the elitism that can lurk in various pockets of triathlon?
  • From free 140.6-mile races and no-drop rides to psychic readings and book clubs (and more book clubs), meet the tri club disruptors who are daring to shake up triathlon by prioritizing inclusion, whole health, and social connection over watts, body exclusivity, and snobbery.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Triathlon club founders and disruptors share how they are building inclusive communities. (Photo: Courtesy Alexa and Branden Scheel, Corinne Geerdts Merten and Melissa Niemuth-Seamonson, Hannah Bradbury, Hilary Topper, and Kyla Lupo).

What do you do when you’re fed up with the elitism that can lurk in various pockets of triathlon? You could throw up your hands in defeat and frustration over the bro culture and inclusion challenges, vowing to train in solitude like a spandex-clad, multisport monk. Or … you could start your own tri club, team, group ride, or clinic.

From free 140.6-mile races and no-drop rides to psychic readings and book clubs (and more book clubs), meet the tri club disruptors who are daring to shake up triathlon by prioritizing inclusion, whole health, and social connection over watts, body exclusivity, and snobbery.

When Altitude Multisport Club, a tri club in Denver, Colorado, was founded in 2010, the board consisted of all men.

It has been revealed that “While friendly, it had a very ‘bro’ vibe and club events were rarely organized by leadership and club meetings were salesy,” says Erin Trail, Altitude Multisport Club’s former president and current volunteer. “What did it for me was a no-drop group ride that the current president and coaching director were on. I had done three Ironman races, and they dropped ME. I knew the route and was fine, but I thought: ‘What if I was a new person? What kind of experience would this be?’”.

Since the president was term-limited, Trail was able to step up as president in 2016 to change the atmosphere to a friendlier, more inclusive one.

Sources indicate that “That first year was very hard. I decided to make the club more inclusive and friendly to beginners and women, eliminating sales or conflict of interest issues and improving communications,” Trail says. “I lost a LOT of club friends because I wanted to make things different. Half my board quit because they didn’t want to be held accountable. But in my first year as president, membership grew from 50 to 150 members!”.

Today, Altitude Multisport Club features winter Sunday pool swims with a coach and travel camps to Moab and a local state park in addition to regular training and racing activities.

Recent findings suggest that “My second term as president was much better, with a diverse board that I handpicked. We added a family membership so households, including kids, could join at a group rate,” Trail says. “And we made it clear that the environment is welcoming, organized, and a safe space to learn for everyone.”.

“A LOT of skinny white men. That’s what I saw in triathlon. I didn’t see enough women, and I really didn’t see anyone who was bigger. I realized that if I wanted to see more folks that looked like me, I had to be the coach that made triathlon a place for all folks, regardless of size, shape, color, or anything else,” indicates Kyla Lupo, who took things into her own hands, getting certified as a coach, learning everything she could, and starting her team, Go Major!, with just one athlete and “a bunch of friends pretending to be my team.” Since then, Go Big! has grown to 22 athletes.

“Our team makes a point to let folks know that they are already loved, exactly as they are. Team Go Substantial! stands for a radical level of body inclusivity, both in sport and the world,” Kyla notes. “On Team Go Big!, we work to overcome our fear and doubts while getting fit and ready for the start line. Anyone can tri in the body they have right now.”.

Sources indicate that social connection is crucial to the Go Significant! community and takes the form of weekly team meetings where members from around the country learn, share their goals, ask for support, and expect accountability.

In a recent development, “We are from all over the country, but there’s a Tuesday morning virtual trainer ride to further connect us. And of course we get to party together at races,” Lupo says.

Disruptors: Alexa and Branden Scheel.

Recent findings suggest that people often join tri clubs to find community, only to discover that they are a small fish in a substantial sea. When you’re one of hundreds of athletes, you and your journey can get lost in the mix.

“My husband, Branden, and I were part of two different teams like that. We felt like ‘just another membership,’” Alexa Scheel states.

Sources indicate that so she and Branden pursued certifications from USA Triathlon and began building the kind of team they actually wanted to be part of. In 2023, the Scheels rolled out Branden Scheel Racing, which focuses on athlete relationships and connection. Despite being a team with athletes around the world, the Scheels strive to make their team feel like family and make each athlete feel seen.

“If we don’t personally know something about each of the team members, we’ve grown too massive, which is why we sit between 100 to 150 members. We are committed to keeping this team on the smaller side,” Scheel says. The beating heart of the team is its Facebook group, where athletes connect through monthly games and seminars, get answers to their most pressing questions, and find encouragement.

“On our team, every athlete stays until the last athlete completes their event because EVERYONE deserves to have someone cheering them on at the finish line. We’ve even had 15 people stay at the finish line for the midnight finish of Ironman Arizona for one of our athletes,” Scheel indicates. “Having a tri family on and off course to cheer for you and celebrate one of the best days of your life is a huge part of our team culture.”.

Disruptors: Jaclyn Fahey, Tara Hofmayer, and Sami Saad.

Fifteen years ago, Jaclyn Fahey started a tri team through a bike store. As it evolved, Fahey recognized the need for a more affordable Long Island-based team, and Landshark Endurance was born.

Sources indicate that “It began as a pizza-and-beer team with a triathlon problem, but Tara and Sami have helped take the lead. Because both are speech therapists and have the gift of gab, they’ve attracted a lot more members,” Fahey states. The open-level, co-ed multisport team supports members of all backgrounds with educational clinics and workshops, group workouts, and of course, social events that revolve around pizza and beer.

According to recent reports, “By sharing our passion and experiences, we hope to show young athletes that success isn’t always measured by winning, but by perseverance, sportsmanship, and the courage to try,” Fahey indicates. “You don’t have to be the fastest or the strongest. You just have to show up for yourself, put in the effort, and enjoy the journey. At the end of the day, the greatest part isn’t always crossing the finish line – it’s the people who help you get there.”.

“I’m non-binary, and when I visit online triathlon groups and ask if there are any fellow non-binary athletes, it’s not uncommon that transphobes will flood the comments. I can only speak for myself, but the fear of discrimination, or being attacked verbally or worse, can be the most intimidating thing for non-binary and trans triathletes about tri clubs,” states Ruth Carter, a lawyer and triathlete. “There’s so much misinformation out there about trans women and non-binary athletes, as well as assumptions that are not supported by research.”.

When Carter couldn’t find a triclub that promoted equal participation and respect, they created Mutants & Masochists, a tri club that believes in equal participation, recognition, and respect for all triathletes, and advocates for non-binary and trans triathletes.

“We’re just getting started, but I hope the club is a place where trans people can connect, both online and in real life,” Carter indicates.

In 2023, Hannah Bradbury was training to break an open-water swim record when she was rushed to the ER for an emergency surgery to remove her gallbladder.

Sources indicate that “My first thought when I woke up was, ‘When can I get back in the water?’ The answer was six weeks at least,” says Bradbury, who had already lost half of her thyroid to cancer in 2017. In an attempt to be part of sport in a way that cancer or a freak surgery couldn’t disrupt, Bradbury created Chicago’s North Avenue Swim and Triathlon Yo (NASTY) Instagram account to post about swimming until she could get back in the water. She also launched book clubs and threw happy hours to create space for people to be more than just athletes, from cancer survivors to diabetic athletes striving to stay in sport on their own terms.

Sources indicate that “Tri and swim clubs are great at training people. They’re not always great at holding onto people when they’re injured, sick, slow, starting over, or just burned out. I wanted to build a club that could hold everyone, from those winning the Chicago Triathlon to anyone rebuilding from injuries, or battling setbacks and the identity crises nobody warns you about when you’re sidelined,” says Bradbury, who faced another cancer scare in 2023. “While I waited on the biopsy, my friends kept me distracted by doing a 100-mile ride with me, covered in glitter, that we called the ride Centuslay.”.

Fortunately, the biopsy came back negative, and the women’s century became an official NASTY tradition every fall.

“Before NASTY I had a hard time making real friends with people who don’t just ask, ‘How was your swim?’ Through NASTY, I met friends who ask how they can show up for me,” Bradbury indicates. “NASTY has grown to over 340 members, and through this community, people have found jobs through a swim or a random happy hour, and even fallen in love. Sport has become an accessory to our friendships, not the glue.”.

According to recent reports, “When I first got into triathlon in 2010, I was fortunate to have a warm, welcoming entry point into the sport. My goal with the T2 community is to pay it forward so others can also ease into the sport, learn to love it, and stay connected for the long haul,” indicates Bryan Mewes, who opened T2 Triathlon & Cycling, a triathlon-focused bike shop in Long Beach, California, in 2023. “The biggest hurdle for beginners is usually being overwhelmed by gear. That and the open-water swim. Once they realize that the shop is a space where they can comfortably ask questions and our group is built on encouragement rather than competition, that anxiety disappears fast.”.

Mewes explains that while it’s easy to say “everyone is welcome,” making sure someone is paired up with a partner at their pace or ensuring no one gets left behind takes actual effort that T2’s committed to making. Beyond the group rides, weekly runs, and bay swims, T2 brings people together off the course and keeps the vibe low-key and welcoming by hosting family dinners at local restaurants, beach days after races, and even a movie club.

Sources indicate that “Some people only do our social events, while others only join our rides. What matters is that they participate in their way and see themselves as part of the community. That’s the core of T2. Training is just the anchor,” Mewes notes.

Disruptors: Ruth Marie Oliver and Team Rocket’s Race Directors and Officers.

Team Rocket Tri Club (TRTC) is on a mission to promote a fit and healthy lifestyle. Every month, the club organizes a themed, post-brick social, and throughout the year, it hosts various races, from a beginner-friendly pool swim to a duathlon and sprint triathlons.

During the summer months, TRTC hosts Tuesday night bricks featuring a multitude of pace groups, ensuring no rider is left behind and everyone has buddies to ride with. And in the winter, the focus is on swim clinics and winter trail running.

“Our club president, Ruth Marie Oliver, has done amazing things, including growing our membership to over 300 people,” claims Cynthia Mitchell, race director of TRTC’s Heel and Crank Duathlon.

Industry observers note that to up the fun factor, TRTC has its own well-traveled bike box that members can borrow, adding their own sticker to its travel history and essentially bringing the whole team along for that athlete’s adventure. There’s also a TRTC hat that is currently “on tour.” It’s been spotted everywhere from Leeds, Alabama, to the head of Bob Babbit in Kona during the Ironman World Championship this year.

Disruptors: Corinne Geerdts Merten and Melissa Niemuth-Seamonson.

In 2019, Corinne Geerdts Merten and Melissa Niemuth-Seamonson relaunched TriBabes WI, a women’s-only, USAT-certified team, to provide a community for women of all abilities and ages to train together.

Sources indicate that “Some women join us purely to have the chance to work out with others for one, two, or all three sports. No matter what the sport or goal, we support each other without all the egos,” Merten says. TriBabesWI makes aspects of triathlon like climbing hills, changing tires, nutrition, and making a race proposal less daunting through the clinics it offers. For TriBabe’s annual team triathlon, athletes can ride with a buddy for the bike portion.

Recent findings suggest that team offerings aren’t limited to the swim-bike-run. There are team hikes, skiing and snowshoeing in the winter, and opportunities to volunteer and shake a cowbell for others.

“We’ve donated our time and efforts to Breakthrough T1D, USAT triathlon events in Milwaukee, Ironman Wisconsin, and naturally Girls on the Run,” Merten says.

“When I was newly introduced to this sport, I went for a bike ride with a triathlon group and got dropped within moments,” notes Topper, an author and coach who started WeREndurance in 2017. “If you’re just starting out, don’t look like everyone else, or just feel different from everyone, many clubs can feel elitist, especially when you get dropped. WeREndurance is nothing like that. It’s inclusive and diverse.”.

As the group’s triathletes grew older and more injury-prone, however, WeREndurance membership began to drop, so Topper proposed transitioning from a strictly triathlon group to a lifestyle group. Now, WeREndurance members who live locally in Long Beach, Fresh York, can participate in monthly hikes and quarterly races, as well as pool parties, holiday parties, diner breakfasts, and even a psychic night. Members who live out of state can stay connected through monthly meditation sessions, a book club, and monthly/bi-monthly educational webinars.

Sources indicate that “These types of activities welcome everyone, including those who are injured or on the sidelines. This builds bonds and social connections,” Topper explains. “As you get older, you realize that sport is not only about being on the podium. It’s about community and having fun with your peers. The social aspect becomes just as notable as training and racing.”.

Disruptors: Brian Masayon, David Bahia, and Kristoffer Crisostomo.

In 2017, Masayon, Crisostomo, Bahia, and six of their friends formed a “silly” club to make training fun, and in doing so, others began taking notice.

“People started reaching out, asking how to join the team. I replied that there was no team. After the 20th inquiry or so, the nine of us decided to open 3P TRI to the public as a fun, drama-free group. That was in October 2017. By the end of the year, we had over 120 members join,” Masayon states. As word spread, the nonprofit tri club’s inclusive vibe attracted members from Canada, Australia, the Philippines, and Mexico.

While Ironman race entries cost athletes between $900 and $1,200, 3P TRI has removed the financial barrier entirely, offering clinics and free 140.6-mile races that are fully supported by the team.

Recent findings suggest that “There is no timing chip, so members are not pressured to prove how fast or slow they are. Instead, they train and then enjoy race day with their teammates,” Masayon claims. For 3P’s 140.6 triathlon, members come from different states to volunteer and help their teammates finish.

“People are intimidated by tri clubs because they have this impression of triathletes as being fast, quick, and strong. Our members, however, come in all shapes and sizes, and this becomes an inspiration to many people,” Masayon adds. “Nobody talks about speed and ability. We don’t play the comparison game.”.

Five years ago, a group of Newly introduced Jersey moms tried a mud run. They had so much fun that one run turned into a road race, followed by group bike rides, and finally dipping their nail-less toes into triathlons, despite the level of intimidation.

It has been revealed that “At a 5K, you’ll see everyone from Boston qualifiers to families participating together, sometimes with little kids in tow. Triathlons can seem like a different world from road or obstacle races. They require training and preparation across three disciplines, and the level of athleticism on display can be intimidating. Sometimes it feels like there are no actual beginners, just really accomplished athletes with super fancy bikes,” claims Merino, adding that if someone indicates up to ride with a mountain bike, they probably know it’s not the fastest option and don’t necessarily need unsolicited advice about upgrading. The same goes for swim form, running technique, or anything else. “If someone asks for pointers, we absolutely help them! Otherwise, the most encouraging thing we can do may be simply making them feel like they belong.”.

“That’s what Team Thunderclap is all about. We might not have the fanciest gear or be the fastest people, but we show up, give it everything we’ve got, and probably laugh a whole lot along the way,” Merino says. “At the end of the day, most of us aren’t competing for Olympic medals. We’re ordinary people doing extraordinary things in our spare time.”.

The 6 Best On Running Shoes for Every Kind of Runner

📅 16 Aug 2018 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1813 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Runnersworld

⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • We earn a commission for products purchased through some links in this article.
  • Editor’s note, November 13, 2026: Presently, this list features the Cloudsurfer 2 and the Cloudsurfer 3.
  • Sources indicate that on has come a long way since the days of cobbling together a running shoe from cut pieces of garden hoses and a dream for a springier shoe.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

We earn a commission for products purchased through some links in this article. Why Trust Us?

Editor’s note, November 13, 2026: Presently, this list features the Cloudsurfer 2 and the Cloudsurfer 3. The Cloudsurfer 3 doesn’t reach full release until February 2027, and the Cloudsurfer 2 is still widely available.

Sources indicate that on has come a long way since the days of cobbling together a running shoe from cut pieces of garden hoses and a dream for a springier shoe. The Swiss shoe manufacturer has evolved into a powerhouse of a brand with design and innovation leading its strategy. Founder and retired athlete Oliver Bernhard, along with Caspar Coppetti and David Allemann, has driven On forward with determination to make exceptional gear that’s high-performing and also sustainable and approachable for runners at all levels of experience and types. Whether you’re a casual road runner or hardcore trail trekker, On wants to match you with one of its pairs.

I have had the opportunity to test several On shoes, as has our Runner-in-Chief Jeff Dengate, alongside runners in our wear-tester program. We have narrowed it down to our favorites that we highlight in this list.

Recent findings suggest that many of the On shoes below have been through our extensive testing process. That means getting each model on the feet of our team of more than 300 avid runners who then put at least 100 miles on the shoe before providing their feedback. We’ve relied on our own in-depth research and experience in the running shoe industry, personal consultation with brand representatives, and nearly a decade of lab data and tester feedback to select the best models below.

On has put in serious work on the upper this time around, and the fit on the Cloudmonster 3 versus the 2 is noticeably more dialed-in, hugging the midfoot without that sloppy, I-might-lose-this-shoe feeling you’d get midrun. The engineered mesh breathes well and moves with—instead of against—your foot.

Fair warning, though, out of the box, the ride is a bit stiff, but give it a couple of runs, and you can sink into it like your favorite hoodie you definitely did not steal from your husband.

Industry observers note that once you’re about 15 miles deep, the CloudTec cushioning opens up and the signature CloudTec pods really carry you, giving you an energetic feel and a snappy return. What surprised me the most was how stable the shoe felt in spite of its impressive stack height. Thanks to the relative firmness of the cushioning, I felt surefooted and stable even on uneven surfaces like gravel and rocky terrain.

Shop Men’s at on.com|Shop Women’s at on.com|On Cloudmonster 3 review.

According to recent reports, at $160, the On Cloudsurfer 2 lands right in the sweet spot of On’s lineup—priced well for a brand that often hits past $170 or $180, and a good value pick if you want On quality without stretching to the top of its usual range. So what does that money get you? A firm ride, first and foremost. This is noticeably firmer than the softer original, so if you’re chasing a super responsive, bouncy daily trainer, this likely isn’t the one to win you over.

According to recent reports, explosive energy return has never been On’s calling card. But that firmness is the whole point. It’s solid, consistent, and thanks to the chunked-up outsole rubber, it’s built to ride those miles. If durability and a dependable, no-drama ride are what you want, the Cloudsurfer 2 has it.

Shop Men’s at on.com|Shop Women’s at on.com.

According to recent reports, if you’re a heel striker looking for protection and comfort on daily runs, the Cloudswift 4 will keep those heel pads from getting wrecked. With a roughly 10mm drop and a 32.7mm heel stack, the geometry naturally favors a rearfoot landing, giving you a smoother heel-to-toe transition. The dual-density Helion midsole layers a softer foam up top for impact absorption over a firmer base for stability, and the newly shortened three-quarter Speedboard plate adds a stable, speedy feel for heel and midfoot strikers.

In a recent development, that said, a couple of caveats. The foam runs firm by 2026 standards, so “cloud-like” oversells it, while it’s great for mid-distance runs; long-haul runners may want more cushion. The engineered-mesh sock upper is breathable and comfortable, though the toebox is on the narrow side.

Shop Men’s at on.com|Shop Women’s at on.com.

This shoe is one of our newly introduced favorites from the brand. It is the first shoe from On featuring their new, proprietary Surreal supercritical foam. It’s been in development for years and now it’s live. It provides what On refers to as “their softest cushioning yet,” and I’d agree. It’s a structured softness that doesn’t lose shape like some marshmallowy foams are wont to do.

According to recent reports, this is a daily trainer with a major stack of foam that’s made to keep long miles easy. It’s not a speed shoe, but it is one of those shoes I can see myself grabbing for again and again because it’s simply just reliable. Gear Editor Amanda Furrer states it’s “near perfect” with “comfort all around.” It’s equally wonderful for runners with wide feet, or runners with high insteps looking for a roomy, secure fit.

Shop Men’s at marathonsports.com | Shop Women’s at marathonsports.com.

Sources indicate that I’ve been wearing and training in these for a few weeks, and I’m a massive fan. They are redesigned from the first model to be lighter, snappier, and less prone to the foam condensing. They have a smooth, natural motion flexibility in the midfoot that allows you to rock forward without instability, and the plate gives you propulsion to see the kick through. Altogether, they’re bouncy and fun, and definitely fast.

The fit is solid for most foot types, but if you have flat or very wide feet, these are not for you. Also, if you have a narrow heel like I do, definitely employ the last lace eyelet for a heel lock, as otherwise you’ll probably get a bit of slip. They’re breathable and airy without feeling like they’re too insubstantial, but the texture of the upper itself does take some getting used to.

Shop Unisex at on.com On Cloudboom Strike 2 Review.

According to recent reports, both Dengate and I agree that this is a helluva shoe. As an ultrarunner, particularly an ultra trail runner, what I wear when I am hitting 50, 75, or 100 miles in the backwoods is critical, and these are my new go-tos for those races.

They have plenty of cushioning, and it’s not quite firm, and not super plush, but Goldilocks-level cushioning that helps you deal with the percussive nature of longhauls over rocky terrain while giving you enough spring to keep up your forward momentum. That reinforced fiberglass Speedboard really does help you power through, helping you at mile “I paid for this.”.

Like the Cloudsoma, it has Helion, CloudTec, and Missiongrip, just more of it, and the 3.5 lugs on the bottom of the Cloudultra Pros can comfortably go between the road and the trail, which is another reason it is so fantastic for ultrarunning.

Sources indicate that the grip is impressive, even on muddy, slippery surfaces, and the upper is extremely breathable and comfortable. However, the mesh is so breathable that sand gets right inside, so save these from marsh trails.

Shop Men’s at on.com|Shop Women’s at on.com.

Competition: On’s racing shoes have snappy Helion HF, a Pebax foam, and rocker shape to glide you through transitions. The supershoes, including their Cloudultra Pro trail shoes, have a fiberglass speedboard that propels without losing stability.

In 2025, On introduced a latest marathon-racing shoe, the LightSpray (LS) version of its Cloudboom Strike. Our editors witnessed On’s robot spraying plastic material as it twirled around the shoe, creating the laceless upper. The shoe was worn by 2025 NYC Marathon women’s champion Hellen Obiri.

Cushioned: On is known for its CloudTec cells, which saw an upgrade for this year’s Cloudmonster 3, which help absorb shock across the trunk.

Support: Their wider bases offer a bit of stability, but they’re not a brand that leans into framing for guidance.

It has been revealed that trail: On’s outsole compound, Missiongrip, is a sticky rubber material that is molded into lug formation for the base of the shoe. Depending on the shoe, it can tackle any manner of terrain.

The reason On was designed to be innovative and bring that “cell” formulation to market.

According to recent reports, cloudTec: This is the bread and butter of On. They utilize open tubes or cells of rubber or foam form sandwiched between the top and outsole. They’re made to act as springs and shock absorption that both cushion and propel.

Speedboard: A light and snappy (typically) fiberglass layer in the midsole designed to help propel you forward while keeping you stable.

Helion: On’s proprietary cushioning material is made from a blend of EVA and OBC (olefin block copolymer) foam that provide you with firmness, responsiveness, and helps legs defeat fatigue.

Helion HF (hyper foam) is a Pebax version used in On’s racing shoes, like the Cloudboom Strike and Cloudmonster Hyper.

How does the Cyclon subscription program work?

Recent findings suggest that once you a become a member and create an account, you can order a pair of Cyclon shoes. You’ll be charged a $30 monthly fee for six months. After this period, you can cancel anytime or swap your shoes when they’re worn out. The payment cycle repeats after the swap.

You can cancel the subscription after the first month (shoes must be unworn and returned within 30 days to get your refund; if you don’t return them you’ll be charged $100).

The Cloud X 4 has an X-shaped Speedboard for forefoot flexion and a midfoot cage for support and lateral stability.

#68486. As a Back-of-the-Pack Runner, I Always Struggled to Run at Different Paces—Until I Tried This Approach

As a Back-of-the-Pack Runner, I Always Struggled to Run at Different Paces—Until I Tried This Approach

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that it was a hot summer afternoon on Cold Soil Road, and I had just finished the “First Speed Run,” a guided run in the Nike Run Club app.
  • It has been revealed that disappointed and discouraged, I checked to see the name of the next guided run, hoping it wouldn’t force me to struggle, yet again, with unrealistic speeds.
  • Fortunately, Coach Cory, who led this particular guided run, never once asked me to check my Fitbit for metrics and pace.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that it was a hot summer afternoon on Cold Soil Road, and I had just finished the “First Speed Run,” a guided run in the Nike Run Club app. It included eight one-minute inter­vals interspersed with one minute of recovery. The virtual coach of that run prescribed different speeds, including a mile pace which was “fast,” a 10K pace which was “faster, but slower than a mile pace,” and the slowest of the three, a marathon pace. No matter how much I tried, I couldn’t run at different paces. Over the course of my various flirtations, romances, and relationships with running, I’d always seemed to move at only two speeds: run and walk.

It has been revealed that disappointed and discouraged, I checked to see the name of the next guided run, hoping it wouldn’t force me to struggle, yet again, with unrealistic speeds. The name? “Find Your Pace.” Excited about this fortuitous opportunity, I pressed download and started this short workout even though I had just struggled through the previous one.

Fortunately, Coach Cory, who led this particular guided run, never once asked me to check my Fitbit for metrics and pace. Instead, he only referred to the Rate of Perceived Exertion, a metric that has been around for decades, but that I had, to be honest, ignored for all of that time. RPE is a purely subjective scale from 1 to 10. Typically, 1 refers to an effort level similar to sitting on your couch (i.e., no effort at all), and running at a 3 is a warmup effort. On the other end of the spectrum is 10, an all-out sprint, a pace you can’t sustain for more than half a minute.

Coach Cory explained that my effort level, or exertion, correlated to a variety of distances. For example, I should strive to run a 10K at an RPE of 6, a 5K at 7, and one mile at 9.

He also suggested that runners connect words to different effort levels—for example, the word “strong” when running at the RPE of 6. Honestly, though? At 6, I thought, This is hard, and at 7, I can’t do this. By the time I reached 9, I thought, I have to stop. Coach Cory, on the other hand, suggested I use the word “epic” to describe my fastest pace. He’s clearly an optimist.

Industry observers note that these were very short intervals, so my breathing and heart rate didn’t rise much. But the difference I felt between this run and my previous runs was notable: I was pushing myself in a way I had never done before. I followed Coach Cory’s instructions back and forth on the same block, and not once did I look at my Fitbit or the app to see how fast I was going, which is what I was instructed to do during my previous runs. The whole exercise was over in 10 minutes. You may be thinking, Well, okay, but how fast were you? Did you actually run at different paces?

Turns out, yes, I did. Even more shocking, I had truly picked up speed during these intervals. My mile pace was 9:21, my 5K was 10:30, and my 10K was 10:54. Faster than I’ve ever run during a training run or race. During that one short workout, I realized I could create different paces based on my effort rather than trying to “find” different paces for each race distance.

Recent findings suggest that I know that might seem like semantics, but the difference is meaningful. “Finding” something isn’t in your control, but “creating” is. When a training plan listed different goal paces, I couldn’t seem to reach them, but when I ran based on my RPE, I was able to distinguish between different efforts, and those effort levels translated to mile, 5K, and 10K paces.

This run was memorable. It gave me a boost to not give up on myself or my training. It let me know what was possible if I kept training. Now when a race plan instructs me to run at a 5K or 10K pace, I don’t worry about the speed metrics. Instead, I focus on my effort. Turns out I can create paces even if I can’t find them.

Donna Raskin has had a long career as a health and fitness writer and editor of books and magazine articles. A certified run coach who has practiced yoga for many years, she also loves to lift weights, dance, and go for long walks with her hound dog, Dolly.

This is What Happens When You Slow Down Long Enough to Be Curious

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish

💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, it’s one thing to know you need to slow things down in your everyday experience of life—to slow your thoughts, your breath, your attention, your scrolling, even your assumptions.
  • Neuroscientists tell us that life changes at the end of our comfort zone.
  • Industry observers note that however, we often decide in advance how things will go, or assume we know how another person is feeling.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, it’s one thing to know you need to slow things down in your everyday experience of life—to slow your thoughts, your breath, your attention, your scrolling, even your assumptions. It’s an entirely different thing to know how to slow down. Longtime mindfulness teacher, yoga therapist, and author Jillian Pransky addresses that disconnect in her recent book, The Power of the Pause: 90 Seconds to Calm, Reset, and Reconnect. In its pages, she explains exactly how pausing can alchemize everyday interactions in ways you’ve probably never considered. The following excerpt from the “Pausing in Our Discomfort Zone” chapter highlights how slowing down can help you experience a more nuanced understanding of not only yourself but those who approach the world from a different perspective than you—and why that can benefit everyone. —Renee Marie Schettler, Editor in Chief, YJ.

Neuroscientists tell us that life changes at the end of our comfort zone. The ability to build new neural pathways is called neuroplasticity, and it happens not only from repeating “new” behaviors, but also when we reach beyond what we know and explore new territories. Whether learning a new skill or facing a fear, your brain actively creates new neural connections, enhancing cognitive abilities, memory, and overall brain health.

Industry observers note that however, we often decide in advance how things will go, or assume we know how another person is feeling. These assumptions can keep us stuck in patterns of behaviors or relationship dynamics that simply strengthen our resistance to change. When we remind ourselves that we have space to change, we often begin to see that there might be more going on than we think. We can open up to paradox, contradiction, and complexity in ways we were not able to before.

It has been revealed that we may realize that no way is the only way. That we don’t need to make anything one way. And that things don’t always have to be precisely the way we want them.

Sources indicate that pausing helps us create support and safety for ourselves, giving us the confidence and courage to go beyond our comfort zone. Gradually titrating, step-by-step, into upcoming territory allows our brain to integrate these changes, leading to our personal growth and evolution.

Dr. Gail Parker, psychologist, international presenter, and author of the self-care book Restorative Yoga for Ethnic and Race-Based Stress and Trauma, emphasizes that curiosity is essential for opening space in our conversations for connection, particularly among disparate groups of people.

Sources indicate that she says, “You can make someone else feel safe when you are curious rather than judgmental, assuming, or indifferent. In the face of listening to others, especially those we don’t know so well or those from another culture, it’s important to remember that we can’t know everything about others or every culture, but what we can do is be curious about others.”.

Listening includes being aware of ourselves and how we feel while conversing with another. In this way, we can learn to notice our own expectations and emotions, stay curious about ourselves, and hold space for ourselves and the other person. Dr. Parker suggests Pausing to check in with ourselves during conversations, with questions like:.

• Am I truly listening? • Am I making assumptions? • Do I have expectations? • What am I feeling?

If we can stay aware of ourselves and curious about our feelings, we won’t get stuck in what we are feeling. “A key to remember is that if we can notice when we are in the stress response, we are not stuck in it,” she claims.

Hala Khouri, author of several books, co-editor of Practicing Liberation: Transformative Strategies for Collective Healing and Systems Change, and co-founder of the social activism organization Off the Mat, Into the World, also emphasizes curiosity as an essential cornerstone for connection in difficult conversations.

Khouri, who is also a therapist, yoga teacher, and somatic experience practitioner, contends that curiosity is not only a portal for going deeper into our conversations, but is also the key to helping us know when it is time to leave a conversation—or not have one at all.

“When we are in conversation with another, I think it is key to ask ourselves, can I be curious right now? If we can’t get curious, that might be a good indicator that we need a break or need to remove ourselves from the conversation or situation, if that is an option,” she notes.

Industry observers note that the main point is that we need to stay connected to ourselves so we can sense our internal state. True listening requires curiosity. If we can’t be curious, that’s essential information for us. And, when we are highly activated in the stress response, we cannot simultaneously be curious. That part of our brain is not accessible when we are in fight-or-flight mode.

Whenever you notice you can’t be curious, take a moment to Pause and care for yourself until you can get your curiosity back.

If we could consciously choose to enter conversations with the intention to Listen—to be curious—to understand the other person’s experience a little bit better, maybe even put ourselves in their shoes, we might be able to learn from people in our lives whose world views are different from ours or even opposed to ours.

It has been revealed that it can be helpful to remember that leading with curiosity rather than certainty doesn’t automatically mean that someone else is right. Or that we are wrong. But it opens a space in which we might connect rather than shut down to each other. The goal is not necessarily to reach agreement with others, but to understand each other. For many, this is a radical idea.

It has been revealed that dr. Parker emphasizes that harmonious relationships require awareness, not agreement. In fact, insisting on an agreement can be a hostile act. She claims that the search for agreement can often lead to arguments because it invalidates the other person’s perspective, whereas the search for understanding dissolves the barriers that result in discord and harm and allows us to get to know one another.

It has been revealed that she explained it like this: “If I need to be right, then I’m not going to be able to listen to you unless you are in agreement with me. And, if I need to be right, it means either you have to agree with me or you’re wrong. The need to be right means that somebody else has to be wrong. Who likes to be wrong? Nobody. Nobody wants to be made to feel like they’re wrong. Making someone wrong will most likely push them into a protective stance. But, when we approach someone with curiosity, it creates a whole fresh opening to make a connection with each other. We might say to them, ‘Tell me more…I’m really interested in that…I never thought about it that way.’”.

When we are in difficult or uncomfortable conversations, can we create space to listen to each other with our differences? Can we create space for communication and connection for its own sake rather than for someone to be right and another to be wrong? How can we learn to understand each other rather than agree? How can we treat each other (and ourselves) better while learning to better understand each other and our different perspectives?

Pausing with the intention to prioritize Listening before speaking helps us regulate our nervous system so that we can not only create this space, but we are also less likely to activate someone else’s stress response. Khouri says, “Imagine two nervous systems on high alert trying to have a conversation, it’s almost impossible! Especially if both parties are vying for being right. If you want to disrupt that pattern, you need to figure out how to self-regulate; part of that is about tolerating the discomfort of disagreeing with someone or being in conflict.”.

“One of the most interesting things I’ve discovered in my work, is that when people feel really, really listened to, they themselves are more willing to try to understand the other person, even when they don’t agree,” continues Khouri. “Through this type of listening, I’ve seen some people with very strong convictions and beliefs loosen their grip on their own fixed ideas and start to open up their perspective or get greater understanding and empathy for a different perspective.”.

According to recent reports, if we can Pause during a contentious situation and shift into curiosity, we might stay in the conversation long enough to ask questions that help us get to know someone, and listen in a way that makes them feel genuinely heard. When people feel heard and acknowledged, they are more likely to feel safe enough to listen in return. If we want to be heard and understood, it often starts with ensuring that the other person feels heard first. This of course takes practice.

The 3 Types of Running Workouts You Need to Train for Your First Half Marathon

📅 14 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (982 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Runnersworld

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Nowhere in any running rulebook does it say you have to train for a 5K or 10K before signing up for a half marathon.
  • Cut to Runner’s World’s 20-week beginner half marathon proposal created by Meg Takacs, CPT, a UESCA-certified running coach and founder of the Movement and Miles app.
  • It balances three key workouts designed to help you build endurance safely, recover well, and get comfortable with longer distances.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Nowhere in any running rulebook does it say you have to train for a 5K or 10K before signing up for a half marathon. As a beginner, 13.1 miles is an awesome way to approach long-distance running. You just need a plan that meets you where you’re at right now and progresses gradually to get you to the starting line feeling strong.

Cut to Runner’s World’s 20-week beginner half marathon proposal created by Meg Takacs, CPT, a UESCA-certified running coach and founder of the Movement and Miles app.

It balances three key workouts designed to help you build endurance safely, recover well, and get comfortable with longer distances. You’ll spread these workouts throughout 20 weeks, which gives you plenty of time to build rather than your typical 10- or 14-week proposal.

According to recent reports, each workout progresses as you move through the plan, so it’s a good idea to familiarize yourself with their basic structure and purpose before you jump into training. Here’s how to get the most out of each workout.

DOWNLOAD YOUR ZERO TO HALF STRATEGY HERE.

In a recent development, run/walks help you build aerobic fitness and endurance gradually. You’ll start with a one-minute run followed by a one-minute walk for 20 minutes total, adding one minute to the run interval every session. With run/walks starting at three times a week, you’ll work up to a 10-mile run/walk in week 16, where you run for 20-minute intervals and walk for two minutes (this is your weekend long run).

In a recent development, do the run intervals at a comfortable, low-intensity pace, meaning you should be able to hold a conversation with a friend the whole time. On a scale of 1 to 10 for rate of perceived exertion (RPE), aim for a 2 to 4 for effort level, with 1 being easy like a walk and 10 meaning all-out effort.

Sources indicate that why it works: This is the backbone of the beginner half marathon blueprint. Run/walk sessions help you build the endurance you need to run farther.

10 x 1 minute walk, 1 minute easy-effort run.

According to recent reports, in week four of this initiative, you’ll start incorporating continuous easy runs, beginning with 25 minutes at a truly easy effort. The longest continuous run you will complete is 8 miles with as few walk breaks as possible by week 17.

Recent findings suggest that throughout the plan, there’s more of a focus on time-based easy runs rather than distance. “For beginners, time on your feet is more vital than mileage in order to get your body gradually acclimated to running,” Takacs previously told Runner’s World.

Why it works: Continuous easy runs help boost endurance and give you the confidence you need to run farther.

Run 25 minutes at an easy effort (RPE 2 to 4), limiting walk breaks as much as possible.

The first of your weekly speed workouts begins in week 3. You’ll complete 400-meter repeats at a moderate effort with two-minute walks in between. Moderate effort is slightly above your easy effort, reaching a 4 to 6 out of 10 RPE. “The goal is to try and run each repeat faster than the last,” Takacs adds.

Recent findings suggest that you should still be able to speak during the work intervals, but you’re breathing heavier and can only talk in phrases. Over the course of the training plan, you’ll work your way up to longer intervals, like 800-meter, 1200-meter, and mile repeats.

Why it works: Speed workouts aren’t just there to help you get faster; they also boost your overall fitness and running economy so easy runs feel easier.

Recent findings suggest that short postrun strides help build speed and leg turnover, and you’ll find them sprinkled throughout your blueprint. These accelerations will help you build more speed, improve your running form by getting your legs to turn over quicker, and boost your confidence.

The goal of strides is to run at a hard effort for 10 to 15 seconds, but it doesn’t have to be an all-out sprint. Aim for a 7 to 10 RPE; you should only be able to say a word or three at a time.

In a recent development, in any training plan, strength workouts are crucial to prevent injury, support your running economy and durability, and get stronger. In this plan, you’ll complete strength workouts once or twice a week before or after your runs. Depending on your preference, you can decide to run in the morning, then follow with strength in the afternoon or evening (or vice versa).

Takacs recommends starting with bodyweight exercises if you’re newly introduced to strength training and then adding in weights as you get stronger.

GET 30-MIN STRENGTH WORKOUTS HERE.

According to recent reports, there’s a reason coaches tell runners to work hard and recover harder. Your recovery days are meant to feel like a true recovery where you can come back to your next run feeling refreshed, strong, and excited to get back out there.

It’s a good idea to loosen stiff muscles with foam rolling, stretching, and some mobility drills. If you need a complete day off, it’s also okay to not do anything at all except watch TV, read a book, or hang out with friends. A day off is good for the mind and the body. This is also a good opportunity to make sure you’re getting to bed early so you can show up to each run as your best, well-rested self.

Sources indicate that kristine Kearns, a writer and avid runner, joined Runner’s World and Bicycling in July 2024. She previously coached high school girls cross country and at the moment competes in seasonal races, with more than six years of distance training and an affinity for weightlifting. You can find her wearing purple, baking cupcakes, and visiting her local farmers market.

6 Tips for Maintaining Your Fitness Routine During the Busy Holiday Season

📅 15 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (966 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Runnersworld

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • The holiday season has arrived, and with it, plenty of reasons your fitness routine may slide.
  • Recent findings suggest that well, consider this: You don’t have to do as much as you think to maintain your fitness between now and Fresh Year’s Day.
  • Researchers also found that, in generally active adults, cutting training frequency to just twice a week for up to 15 weeks could maintain short-term endurance and VO₂ max.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The holiday season has arrived, and with it, plenty of reasons your fitness routine may slide. Between shopping for gifts, attending holiday parties, and meeting work obligations, it can feel like there’s not enough time to squeeze in an hour-long workout session—so why even try?

Recent findings suggest that well, consider this: You don’t have to do as much as you think to maintain your fitness between now and Fresh Year’s Day. A review published in the Journal of Strength and Conditioning Research in 2021 suggests that you can reduce your workout time by two-thirds and still maintain your gains, as long as the intensity stays the same.

Researchers also found that, in generally active adults, cutting training frequency to just twice a week for up to 15 weeks could maintain short-term endurance and VO₂ max.

Setting an attainable goal for yourself, like running for at least 30 minutes two or three times per week, can make staying active through the holidays feel more doable. It’s how I was able to get back to exercise after a break, and it’s also how I blueprint to maintain my fitness this winter—in addition to following some of the best advice from my Runner’s World colleagues.

So ditch the all-or-nothing mindset and use the following tips to your advantage now, so when the New Year arrives, you’ll be ready to tackle your goals for 2027.

“I have a race in mid-January, so I am following a training strategy [which keeps me motivated]. But I am also cross-training with step aerobics, and I’ve added jump training into my workouts. I was bored with my usual strength routine, so I decided to mix things up with kettlebell training, targeting my upper body and core.” —Donna Raskin, senior health and fitness editor.

“I make time for newly introduced workout classes, like the ones offered by Solidcore and OrangeTheory to support my strength needs, because I usually don’t get to attend those sessions when I’m training for a race.” —Sara Hemstock, senior director of marketing and brand liaison.

“I love doing strength work and some form of speed training in the winter. I recently found an indoor track in my local YMCA, and I’m excited to use that as an option for when it snows. There’s something nostalgic about it for me after running winter track as a kid.” —Kristine Kearns, associate health and fitness editor.

It has been revealed that “I love running on Christmas Day because it’s always so quiet in my hometown of Columbia, South Carolina. I usually run downtown, past the state capitol building, and through the University of South Carolina. The normally busy area turns into a complete ghost town! It’s a once-a-year experience and a personal tradition. I look forward to it every year.” —Theo Khaler, news editor.

“Every year, I look forward to going home to North Carolina during the holidays because I get to test my fitness in my neighborhood Turkey Trot. It’s a community event put on by my high school, and it always draws a huge crowd.

In a recent development, the 5K race itself gives me something to look toward and train for in the fall. It’s a great chance to test my speed and have fun with the sport, but the best part has to be the community aspect. I catch up with old friends, teammates, coaches, teachers, and neighbors, and hearing about their own running journeys always fuels mine, too. Plus, each age-group winner wins a pie. Who doesn’t like free dessert?” —Ashley Tysiac, content hype editor.

“I motivate myself by thinking of all the folks who decided not to run as I was bundled up, gutting out a sub-freezing effort. It just makes me feel proud thinking that I decided to lace up and get out the door that particular day when someone else may not have.

The thought process works both ways: If I decide to skip a cold-weather run, I think about all the people who are out there toughing it out while I’m sipping hot chocolate on my couch.” —Matt Rudisill, associate service editor.

Recent findings suggest that “This is the time of year when I try to add strength work into my routine because I am usually indoors at the gym more. But I find strength training so boring, so I experiment with different protein shakes to find the ones I really like, which keeps me motivated. I consider them a postworkout treat!” —Amanda Furrer, running reviews editor.

According to recent reports, “I treat myself to nice, upcoming running clothes, and that makes cold weather running more enjoyable. I also like testing out new looks. It gives me something to look forward to.”—Hemstock.

“Indoor workouts allow me to experiment with different outfits, like a shirt with comfortable sweatpants or oversized sweatsuits. That makes me feel really cozy and confident so I want to keep on training.” —Kearns.

“I try to run at least a mile every day through the holidays, like a running streak. It can be inside or outside.” —Furrer.

“I give myself permission to shorten any and all workouts. Even if I just commit to 20 minutes, I usually end up doing more, but knowing I can stop early breaks down the barrier to getting started.” —Mallory Creveling, deputy editor, health and fitness.

Monique LeBrun is a health and fitness editor who is based in Easton, Pennsylvania. She covers a wide range of health and wellness topics, with a primary focus on running performance and nutrition. Monique is passionate about creating content that empowers runners to become the best versions of themselves. As an avid runner and parent, she loves spending time outdoors with her daughter, who often accompanies her on weekend runs as her personal mini run coach.

#68477. Industry News: Reviewed: The EZ Hydro-Glide Swim Cap

📅 19 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (1070 w)
